# Software

`customer_support.offering.product.software` · offering_type · parent `customer_support.offering.product`

> Software sold as a running service or as an installed application. The defining structural fact is that we hold the source and, in the hosted case, the deployment: we can make the fault stop without the customer doing anything at all, and their only obligation is to wait. That is the strongest position in support and it quietly shapes every conversation. Expectation-setting stops being a negotiation and becomes a statement about our own release train; the honest answer to "when" is a date we control; and a promise made here is a promise we can actually keep unilaterally, which is why software support tolerates specific commitments that would be reckless in any other branch of this tree. It inverts the moment the software is self-hosted. The fix is still ours, but landing it needs the customer's change window, their regression testing and their approval — so a self-hosted ticket is a customer-environment job wearing a software label, and every resolution is a negotiation about an upgrade the customer has reasons to refuse. Operators who move from hosted to on-premise keep quoting fix dates out of habit and keep being wrong by a quarter, because they are quoting the date the code was ready rather than the date it ran anywhere. Volume is release-shaped, and the release calendar is ours. A support function that is not told about deploys is being asked to predict the weather without a window.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| delivery | continuously running and updated by us on our own cadence when hosted; versioned builds the customer installs when self-hosted — two different offerings sharing a codebase |
| pricing_shape | per-seat or usage-based recurring; support is bundled into the subscription, so it appears as a cost against renewal rather than as a revenue line |
| margin_profile | high gross margin, which means cost-to-serve per account is the variable that decides whether a whole segment is profitable — the cheapest plan can be the one losing money |
| post_sale_load | continuous; the product is consumed every day and the renewal is decided by the accumulated experience of that, not by the last ticket |
| support_load | a steady baseline proportional to active users, with sharp correlated spikes on our own release boundaries and on third-party changes nobody scheduled with us. A single bad deploy puts the entire install base in the queue within the hour, so the incident path here is a volume path and not an exception |
| resolution_locus | our codebase, deployed by us — we can fix it unilaterally and the customer's only job is to wait. Self-hosted inverts it: the code is ours, the change window is theirs, and the ticket sits in `waiting_on_customer` while looking exactly like an open defect |
| notes | Hosted and self-hosted are close enough commercially to be sold as one SKU and far enough apart operationally that a queue mixing them without a flag will systematically misjudge every fix-date question it is asked.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `resolution_type`, `verified_by_customer`, `reopen_count`


> These three exist to stop the most expensive lie in software support: closing on a workaround and recording it as a fix. `resolution_type` says what actually made the problem stop, `verified_by_customer` says whether anyone but us believes it, and `reopen_count` is the only field that catches the pattern where the same ticket is closed three times by three agents who each thought they were first.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.incident`

Requires `status_page_published`, `last_broadcast_at`, `sla_clock_policy`


> With a shared install base, silence is itself a message and the queue that fills during an incident is proportional to how long it lasted. `sla_clock_policy` is required because incident-covered tickets otherwise breach en masse against clocks nobody intended to run, and the resulting credit exposure is discovered by finance weeks later.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.knowledge_article`

Requires `verified_against_version`, `last_verified_at`


> In self-hosted estates several versions are live at once and the customer's version is rarely the newest. An article that does not say what it was verified against is not just stale, it is unsafe to serve to an audience whose version we cannot see.
